etymology: From the Latin Clemens, “merciful” or “mild,” the name of the head of the catechetical school of Alexandria, c.150–215 AD.
biblical_def: Titus Flavius Clemens, called Clement of Alexandria, was an early Christian teacher who about the year 190 took charge of the catechetical school of Alexandria, that great seat of learning where the faith was taught to converts out of the heathen world. He wrote much in defence of Christ against the pagan philosophers and the rising heresies of his day; his chief works are the Exhortation to the Greeks, the Tutor, and the Stromata, or miscellanies, in which he laboured to commend the gospel to the educated mind of his age. The dictionary honours Clement for his early defence of the faith when the church was small and pressed on every side, and for his clear teaching that all true knowledge is subordinate to faith in Christ, who is the Word of God. He held that the believer should not fear learning but bring it captive to Christ, for the apostle bids us beware lest any man spoil us through philosophy and vain deceit, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ (Col 2:8). Clement strove, however imperfectly, to wield knowledge in the service of the faith once delivered, and to lead the heathen from their idols to the living God who hath in these last days spoken unto us by His Son (Heb 1:2). His school nurtured Origen after him, and his witness stands among the early teachers who contended for Christ before the creeds were framed.
webster_summary: An early Christian teacher and head of the catechetical school of Alexandria, who defended the faith against the heathen.
webster_full: CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA, an early Christian teacher of the second and third centuries.

His speculative Platonizing allegory strayed from the plain sense of Scripture.

For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
corruption_summary: An early teacher who defended the faith, yet whose Platonizing allegory and “true gnostic” ideal strayed from the plain sense of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Clement is honoured for his early defence of Christ and for subordinating all learning to faith; the dictionary records what is honourable in him, that he stood for the gospel against the heathen philosophers in a hard and early day.

Yet his error must be named. Clement was a Platonizing teacher who read the plain words of Scripture through the allegorizing method of the Greek schools, dissolving the literal sense into a hidden spiritual meaning of his own devising. Worse, he set up the ideal of the “true gnostic,” a higher Christian who rises by knowledge above the simple believer to a secret and superior wisdom. This proto-gnostic conceit corrupts the apostolic word, for Paul warns that knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1), and that it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe, not by a hidden wisdom reserved for the learned. The plain sense of the text, not the allegory of the philosophers, is the rule of faith; and the gospel is one for the babe and the sage alike. Clement’s speculation seeded the still graver allegorism of Origen who followed him, and the dictionary marks the strain it loosed as a departure from the sound and literal handling of the word of God.

etymology: From the Latin Cyprianus, “of Cyprus,” the name of the bishop of Carthage who was martyred under Valerian, c.200–258 AD.
biblical_def: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, called Cyprian of Carthage, was bishop of that great African city in the middle of the third century, and a leader of the Western church in a day of fierce persecution. Converted in mature years out of a life of rhetoric and worldly honour, he gave himself wholly to Christ, and as a shepherd he laboured to guide the flock through the storms of the Decian and Valerian persecutions, when many fell away under torture and the church wrestled how to receive the lapsed who repented. Cyprian counselled mercy joined to discipline, that the penitent be restored in order and not lightly. At the last he was himself called to the crown he had urged on others: under Valerian he was beheaded for the name of Christ in the year 258, and so was found faithful unto death. The dictionary honours Cyprian for his courage, his pastoral discipline, and his martyrdom, for the Lord saith, Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life (Rev 2:10). He counted not his life dear, that he might finish his course with joy, and the ministry which he had received of the Lord Jesus (Act 20:24). His blood, like that of the early witnesses, watered the church; and his steadfastness under the sword stands as a true testimony of the grace that upholds the saints in the day of trial, to whom it is given not only to believe, but also to suffer for Christ’s sake (Phi 1:29).
webster_summary: The bishop of Carthage, martyred under Valerian, honoured for his courage and pastoral discipline.
webster_full: CYPRIAN OF CARTHAGE, bishop of Carthage in the third century.
He was converted in mature years and gave himself wholly to Christ.
He guided the church through the Decian and Valerian persecutions.
He was beheaded for the name of Christ under Valerian in 258.
His sacerdotal view of the church Rome later built upon.

corruption_summary: A courageous martyr-bishop, yet whose sacerdotal episcopate and “no salvation outside the church” formula Rome later built upon.
corruption_paragraphs: Cyprian is honoured for his courage, his pastoral care of a flock under persecution, and his martyrdom under Valerian; the dictionary records what is honourable in him, that he was faithful unto death and sealed his witness with his blood.

Yet his error must be named. Cyprian taught a sacerdotal view of the episcopate, making the bishop a priest in succession and the visible church, bound to that office, the one ark of salvation. From him comes the formula extra ecclesiam nulla salus, “no salvation outside the church,” understood of the visible, episcopal church; and from him the saying that he cannot have God for his Father who hath not the church for his mother. Upon this Rome later built her whole structure of priestly mediation and papal claim. But Scripture knows no priesthood set between Christ and the believer save the one High Priest, the Lord Jesus, and the royal priesthood of all the saints (1Pe 2:9). The true church is the company of the elect, known to God, and salvation is found in Christ alone by faith, not in submission to a visible hierarchy. Cyprian’s sacerdotalism confounded the sign with the thing signified, and the dictionary names it as the seed of the sacramental and papal corruptions the Reformation called the church away from.

etymology: From the Greek eklekte kyria, “elect lady,” the recipient to whom the apostle John addressed his second epistle.
biblical_def: The elect lady is the recipient to whom the apostle John addressed his second epistle, a Christian woman, or by some a Christian household or church figured as a lady, whom the apostle loved in the truth. He opens, The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth; and not I only, but also all they that have known the truth (2Jo 1:1). He rejoiced greatly that he found of her children walking in truth, as we have received a commandment from the Father (2Jo 1:4), and he wrote to beseech her that we love one another, and to walk after His commandments (2Jo 1:5-6). He warned her also against the deceivers who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh, charging that she receive not such into her house, neither bid him God speed (2Jo 1:10). The dictionary marks the elect lady as a true believer commended for the twin marks of the Christian life, truth and love, walking in the truth and abounding in love within the bounds the truth sets. Her election, named in her very title, was the spring of her faithfulness, for whom He did predestinate, them He also called (Rom 8:30). She stands as a witness that the godly woman, ordering her house in the faith and guarding her children and her door against false teachers, fulfils a real and honoured place in the church of Christ, and that to walk in truth and love is the whole sum of obedience the apostle requires.
webster_summary: The Christian woman or household to whom John addressed his second epistle, commended for walking in truth and love.
webster_full: THE ELECT LADY, the recipient of the apostle John’s second epistle.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the elect lady witnesses to a godly woman walking in truth and love and guarding her house from error.
corruption_paragraphs: The elect lady has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the honoured recipient of John’s second epistle. The dictionary records her that the reader may mark the twin graces of truth and love for which the apostle commends her.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that truth and love together are the whole walk of the Christian, and that the godly woman has a real and honoured calling to order her house in the faith. The elect lady walked in the truth and abounded in love, yet her love was bounded by the truth, so that she shut her door against the deceivers who denied that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh. So the saint is taught that charity does not bid God speed to error, and that to guard the household and the children against false teaching is itself an act of love. Her very title marks her election as the spring of her faithfulness; for the called walk in truth because the Father first set His love upon them.

etymology: From the Greek Demetrios, “belonging to Demeter,” the name of a faithful disciple commended in the apostle John’s third epistle.
biblical_def: Demetrius was a disciple commended by the apostle John in his third epistle, a man so well reported of that the apostle held him up as a pattern to Gaius, to whom he wrote. He saith of him, Demetrius hath good report of all men, and of the truth itself: yea, and we also bear record; and ye know that our record is true (3Jo 1:12). A threefold witness is borne to him: the witness of all men, who saw his walk; the witness of the truth itself, with which his life agreed; and the witness of the apostle, whose record is true. Likely he was the bearer of the epistle, or one whom John sent and would have the church receive, in contrast to Diotrephes, who loved to have the preeminence and received not the brethren. The dictionary marks Demetrius as the faithful witness whose life and doctrine bore one testimony, for he had good report of the truth itself, his conduct being a living agreement with the gospel he professed. He stands for the believer of whom the world and the church alike can speak well, walking so as to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things (Tit 2:10). The apostle bade Gaius, Follow not that which is evil, but that which is good (3Jo 1:11); and Demetrius was set before him as that good to follow, a plain man of unblemished report, whose quiet faithfulness was honour enough that an apostle should name it in the Scripture of God.
webster_summary: A faithful disciple commended in John’s third epistle, who had good report of all men and of the truth itself.

corruption_paragraphs: Demetrius has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the disciple of good report in John’s third epistle. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the threefold witness borne to his faithful walk.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a good name, won by a life that agrees with the truth professed, is rather to be chosen than great riches. Demetrius had good report of all men, and of the truth itself; his conduct and his confession bore one testimony, so that the apostle could set him before Gaius as the good to follow. So the saint is taught to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things, that his walk may bear record to the gospel he holds; for he that doeth good is of God, and a faithful disciple’s quiet integrity is honour enough that the Spirit should write his name in the Scripture.

etymology: From the Greek Nikolaos, “conqueror of the people,” a proselyte of Antioch chosen among the seven to serve tables.
biblical_def: Nicolas was a proselyte of Antioch, one of the seven men chosen by the church at Jerusalem to serve tables, when the daily ministration to the widows had been neglected and the apostles would not leave the word of God to serve tables (Act 6:2). The multitude chose seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, and among them Stephen and Philip and the rest, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch (Act 6:5). These the apostles set apart with prayer and the laying on of hands, that they might oversee the temporal care of the saints while the apostles gave themselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word (Act 6:4). The dictionary marks Nicolas among the first servants, or deacons, of the church, and notes that he was a proselyte, a Gentile who had been brought to the God of Israel and then to Christ, a sign of the gospel reaching beyond the natural seed of Abraham. His appointment, with the rest, teaches the church to order her mercy-ministry under godly men of honest report, that the word may not be hindered and the needy not neglected. The choosing of the seven, and the office it founded, is honoured of the dictionary as the New Testament pattern for the deacon, that all things be done decently and in order (1Co 14:40), and that the saints be served in body while the ministers serve them in the word.
webster_summary: A proselyte of Antioch, one of the seven chosen to serve tables in the early church at Jerusalem.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; Nicolas witnesses to the founding of the deacon’s office for the ordered care of the saints.
corruption_paragraphs: Nicolas has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the seven first servants of the church. A tradition of later times would link his name to the Nicolaitanes whose deeds the Lord hated (Rev 2:6, 15); but the Scripture makes no such charge, and the connection is uncertain and not to be pressed against a man whom the church chose as of honest report.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the godly ordering of the church’s mercy-ministry, that the needy be served and the word not hindered. The seven, Nicolas among them, were chosen as men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, and set apart with prayer and the laying on of hands; so the office of the deacon was founded for the temporal care of the saints while the elders give themselves to prayer and the word. That Nicolas was a proselyte witnesses to the gospel reaching beyond the natural seed of Abraham; and the dictionary honours the decent and orderly governing of the household of God, where all things are done decently and in order.

etymology: From the Hebrew Tselophchad, the name of a man of Manasseh; his five daughters were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.
biblical_def: The daughters of Zelophehad were five women of the tribe of Manasseh, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah, whose father died in the wilderness leaving no son. When Israel was about to divide the land by inheritance, they came near before Moses and the priest and the princes, saying, Our father died in the wilderness, and had no sons; why should the name of our father be done away from among his family, because he hath no son? Give unto us therefore a possession among the brethren of our father (Num 27:3-4). And Moses brought their cause before the LORD; and the LORD said unto Moses, The daughters of Zelophehad speak right: thou shalt surely give them a possession of an inheritance among their father’s brethren (Num 27:7). From this a statute and a judgment was established in Israel concerning inheritance where there is no son. Afterward, that the inheritance not pass from tribe to tribe, they were charged to marry within their own tribe (Num 36:6), and so it was done, and their inheritance remained in Manasseh; and Joshua gave them their portion among their kinsmen (Jos 17:3-6). The dictionary marks the daughters of Zelophehad as women who sought their lawful inheritance in faith and order, not in rebellion but by coming meekly before the appointed authority; and the LORD, who is no respecter of persons, ordered the law justly to provide for them. Their case witnesses to the equity of God’s law, that careth for the daughter and the widow and the man without a son, ordering all things in righteousness.
webster_summary: Five daughters of Manasseh who sought their father’s inheritance, and for whom God ordered the law of inheritance justly.

corruption_paragraphs: The daughters of Zelophehad have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the women whose cause established a statute of inheritance in Israel. The dictionary records them that the reader may mark the meekness of their suit and the justice of God’s answer.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the perfect equity of God’s law, which careth for the daughter and the man without a son and orders all things in righteousness. These women came not in rebellion but meekly before the appointed authority, Moses and the priest and the princes, and laid their cause before the LORD; and He, who is no respecter of persons, judged that they spake right and gave them their inheritance. Yet that the inheritance not wander from tribe to tribe, He bound them to marry within their own people, ordering provision and order together. So the dictionary honours the law of the LORD as just and good, and these daughters as faithful women who sought their right in faith, submission, and order.

etymology: From the Hebrew Abel, “meadow” or “mourning,” the city Abel of Beth-maachah whose wise woman saved it by counsel.
biblical_def: The wise woman of Abel was an unnamed woman of the city of Abel of Beth-maachah, who in the days of David saved her city by her wisdom. When Sheba the son of Bichri raised a revolt against David and fled to Abel, Joab came up and besieged the city, casting up a bank against the wall to throw it down. Then cried a wise woman out of the city, and called for Joab, and said, Hear, hear; say, I pray you, unto Joab, Come near hither, that I may speak with thee (2Sa 20:16). She pleaded that Abel was a city and a mother in Israel, peaceable and faithful, and asked, Why wilt thou swallow up the inheritance of the LORD? (2Sa 20:19). Joab answered that he sought not to destroy, but only the rebel Sheba; and the woman said, Behold, his head shall be thrown to thee over the wall (2Sa 20:21). Then the woman went unto all the people in her wisdom; and they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and cast it out to Joab, and the siege was lifted and the city saved. The dictionary marks the wise woman of Abel as a deliverer by counsel, who by understanding and persuasion saved a whole city and turned away the sword. Her wisdom teaches that the word fitly spoken and the counsel of understanding are mighty to deliver, for wisdom is better than weapons of war (Ecc 9:18), and a wise woman in her place may save a multitude by the word of peace.
webster_summary: An unnamed wise woman who saved Abel of Beth-maachah by counsel, delivering up the rebel Sheba.

corruption_paragraphs: The wise woman of Abel has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the counsellor who saved her city from Joab’s siege. The dictionary records her that the reader may mark the power of wise counsel to turn away the sword.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that wisdom is better than weapons of war, and that the word fitly spoken is mighty to deliver. When Joab’s bank rose against the wall, no army came to Abel’s rescue; but a wise woman, pleading for a city and a mother in Israel, parleyed with the captain, learned his true aim, and persuaded the people to deliver up the one rebel. So a whole city was saved and the inheritance of the LORD spared. The dictionary honours her understanding, and draws the lesson that God may make the counsel of one wise soul the means of saving many, and that peace sought through wisdom may accomplish what no force of arms could win.

etymology: From the Hebrew Tsarephath, “smelting place,” a city of Sidon where a widow fed the prophet Elijah.
biblical_def: The widow of Zarephath was a Gentile woman of the coasts of Sidon to whom the LORD sent Elijah in the great famine, that she should sustain him. When the prophet came to the gate, she was gathering sticks to dress a last meal for herself and her son, that they might eat it and die; for she had but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse. But Elijah said, Fear not; make me thereof a little cake first, for the barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth (1Ki 17:14). She believed and did according to his word, and she, and he, and her house, did eat many days; and the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail (1Ki 17:16). Afterward, when her son fell sick and died, Elijah cried unto the LORD, and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived (1Ki 17:22). The dictionary marks the widow of Zarephath as a Gentile woman of faith, who out of her poverty fed the prophet and received life for life. Our Lord named her, that many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias, but unto none was he sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow (Luk 4:25-26), a sign that the grace of God reaches beyond Israel to the believing Gentile, and that He honours the faith that ventures all upon His word.
webster_summary: A Gentile widow of Sidon who fed Elijah from a barrel of meal that wasted not, and whose son was raised.
webster_full: THE WIDOW OF ZAREPHATH, a Gentile widow of Sidon in the days of Elijah.
She had but a handful of meal and a little oil in the famine.
By the word of the LORD her barrel and cruse did not fail.
She fed Elijah, herself, and her house many days.
Her son died and was raised by the prophet’s prayer.
scriptures: For thus saith the LORD God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth.
And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Elijah.
And the LORD heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.
Luk 4:26

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the widow of Zarephath witnesses to the faith that ventures all on God’s word, and to grace reaching the Gentile.
corruption_paragraphs: The widow of Zarephath has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Gentile woman who fed Elijah and saw the meal and oil not fail. The dictionary records her that the reader may mark her faith and the mercy shown her.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faith that ventures all upon the bare word of God, and the sovereign grace that reaches beyond Israel to the believing Gentile. At the point of death she gave her last morsel to the prophet at his word, and the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail; and when her son died, the LORD heard Elijah and raised him. Our Lord named her in the synagogue at Nazareth to show that grace was never bound to natural Israel, but flowed where God willed, even to a widow of Sidon. So the dictionary honours her as a pattern of the faith that trusts God’s promise against all sight, and a foretaste of the gospel going forth to the nations.
roots_summary: From Zarephath in Sidon, the widow is marked who fed Elijah and saw her son raised.

usage: Like the widow of Zarephath, faith ventures its last morsel upon the word of God.
The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail.
Grace was never bound to Israel, but reached even a widow of Sidon.

etymology: From the Hebrew Qish, perhaps “bow” or “a snare,” a Benjamite, the father of Saul the first king of Israel.
biblical_def: Kish was a Benjamite of the tribe of Benjamin, the father of Saul who became the first king of Israel. The Scripture names him a mighty man of power: Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bechorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power (1Sa 9:1). He had a son named Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly, taller than any of the people from his shoulders and upward (1Sa 9:2). It was a small and ordinary matter that brought Saul to the kingdom: the asses of Kish his father were lost, and Kish said to Saul his son, Take now one of the servants with thee, and arise, go seek the asses (1Sa 9:3). In that errand Saul sought the asses and found a kingdom, for the seeking led him to Samuel, who anointed him king at the LORD’s command. The dictionary marks Kish as the father whose lost asses, by the secret providence of God, sent his son to the prophet and so to the throne of Israel. His small household trouble was the very means God used to bring about the thing He had purposed; for the LORD ordereth the steps of a man (Pro 16:9), and turneth even the seeking of strayed beasts to the raising up of a king. So Kish witnesses to the providence of God, which worketh through the least and most common affairs of men to accomplish His appointed ends.
webster_summary: A Benjamite, a mighty man of power, the father of Saul; his lost asses sent Saul to Samuel.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; Kish witnesses to the providence of God, which works through the least affairs to accomplish His ends.
corruption_paragraphs: Kish has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Benjamite father of Saul whose lost asses set the story of the first king in motion. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the providence that worked through so small a matter.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God, which orders the least and most common affairs of men to accomplish His appointed ends. The asses of Kish were lost, an ordinary household trouble; yet by the seeking of them Saul was led to Samuel, and so to the throne God had purposed for him. A man’s heart deviseth his way, but the LORD directeth his steps. So the dictionary honours the secret governance of God in small things, and teaches that no event is too trifling for His hand to use, who turneth even a strayed beast and a son’s errand to the raising up of a king and the working out of His will.

etymology: From the Hebrew Heman, “faithful” or “trusty,” a Levitical singer and the king’s seer, set over the song in the house of the LORD.
biblical_def: Heman was a Levite of the sons of Kohath, a singer appointed by David and the king’s seer, set with Asaph and Jeduthun over the song in the house of the LORD. When the ministers of music were ordained, the singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were appointed to sound with cymbals of brass (1Ch 15:17, 19), and David and the captains of the host separated to the service the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals (1Ch 25:1). Heman is called the king’s seer in the words of God, and God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters; all these were under the hands of their father for song in the house of the LORD (1Ch 25:5-6). His name stands also in the title of the eighty-eighth Psalm, A Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite, the darkest of the songs, a prayer out of the depths of affliction. The dictionary marks Heman as a chief of the temple-singers and a seer, whose office joined music and prophecy in the worship of God; for the song of the sanctuary was no mere ornament but a prophetic ministry, that the saints might sing with grace in their hearts to the Lord (Col 3:16). His house, set apart for praise, teaches that worship is a holy and ordered service, appointed of God and committed to His servants, and that even the song of deepest grief, as in his psalm, is offered up unto the LORD who heareth the cry of the afflicted.
webster_summary: A Levitical singer and the king’s seer, set over the song in the house of the LORD.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; Heman witnesses to the ordered, prophetic ministry of song in the worship of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Heman has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a chief of the temple-singers and the king’s seer. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the holy office of song appointed in the house of the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship is a holy and ordered service, appointed of God and committed to His servants, and that the song of the sanctuary is a prophetic ministry, not a mere ornament. Heman was set over the song with Asaph and Jeduthun, and is called the king’s seer; his sons prophesied with harps and psalteries and cymbals. So the dictionary honours the place of godly music in worship, that the word of Christ dwell richly in the saints, who sing with grace in their hearts to the Lord. And the eighty-eighth Psalm, the darkest of all, bearing his name, teaches that even the song of deepest affliction is offered up to the LORD who heareth the cry of His own.
